item.description:
Authors: Cæcilie Stilling Denholt, Hannah K. Wood-Kurland, Kathrine Kold Sørensen, Marcella Broccia, Kristian Kragholm, Thomas Alexander Gerds, Christian Torp-Pedersen, Mikkel Porsborg Andersen
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2639072
Abstract: Importance Low socioeconomic status is associated with increased risk of cardiovascular disease, yet it remains unclear whether this association has changed over time. Major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) are key contributors to cardiovascular morbidity, mortality, and health care costs and, thus, are indicators of the overall cardiovascular burden. Objective To describe temporal trends in incident MACE by equivalized income groups in the Danish population from 1988 to 2023. Design, Setting, and Participants This nationwide, population-based open cohort study using data from Danish national registries included all residents of Denmark aged 30 years or older who were alive in each year between January 1, 1988, and January 1, 2023, and had available income observations in the current or preceding 5 years. Individuals were followed up to December 31 of each year, to death, or to emigration. Data were analyzed from August 2025 to July 2026. Exposure Equivalized disposable household income. Main Outcome and Measures Incident MACE, defined as the first hospital admission for acute myocardial infarction, unstable angina, stroke, or heart failure. Age-standardized incidence rates were calculated annually, stratified by income quartile and sex. Results A total of 5 932 672 individuals aged 30 years or older were registered in the Danish Civil Registration System from 1988 to 2023. The annual study population increased from 3.06 million in 1988 to 3.85 million in 2023. Most residents in 1988 were female (52.1%), and most in 2023 were male (51.1%); the median age increased from 50.8 years (IQR, 40.2-65.6 years) in 1988 to 55.8 years (IQR, 43.3-68.8 years) in 2023. Age-standardized incidence rates of MACE decreased across all income groups from 1988 to 2023 but remained highest in the lowest income quartile. For males, the rate decreased from 191.1 (95% CI, 186.3-196.0) per 10 000 person-years to 119.6 (95% CI, 116.0-123.2) per 10 000 person-years in the lowest income quartile, while in the highest quartile it decreased from 153.5 (95% CI, 142.9-164.0) per 10 000 person-years to 85.9 (95% CI, 81.2-90.6) per 10 000 person-years. For females, the rate decreased from 116.0 (95% CI, 113.0-118.9) per 10 000 person-years to 70.4 (95% CI, 68.1-72.6) per 10 000 person-years in in the lowest income quartile and from 89.5 (95% CI, 81.9-97.2) per 10 000 person-years to 53.1 (95% CI, 49.0-57.1) per 10 000 person-years in the highest. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of Danish residents aged 30 years or older from 1988 to 2023, the incidence of MACE declined across all socioeconomic groups. Although individuals with lower income generally experienced higher incidence rates, the overall decline occurred in all socioeconomic groups.

item.title: Ultraprocessed Food Intake and Adiposity, Vascular Brain Injury, and Cognition in Middle-Aged Adults
item.dc:creator: Russell J. de Souza
Karleen M. Schulze
Dipika Desai
Jean-Pierre Després
Trevor J. B. Dummer
Matthias G. Friedrich

Vikki Ho
item.description:
Authors: Russell J. de Souza, Karleen M. Schulze, Dipika Desai, Jean-Pierre Després, Trevor J. B. Dummer, Matthias G. Friedrich, Jason Hicks, Vikki Ho, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2639118
Abstract: Importance Ultraprocessed foods (UPFs) account for a substantial and increasing proportion of dietary intake in Canada. Although UPFs are consistently associated with adiposity and cardiometabolic disease, their associations with subclinical vascular brain injury (VBI) and cognitive performance in midlife are unclear. Objective To evaluate associations of UPF consumption with adiposity, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)–defined VBI, and cognitive performance in middle-aged adults in Canada. Design, Setting, and Participants This cross-sectional study included 8783 adults aged 35 to 69 years without cardiovascular disease who were enrolled in the Canadian Alliance for Healthy Hearts and Healthy Minds (CAHHM) and Prospective Urban and Rural Epidemiology-MIND (PURE-MIND) studies. Participants from CAHHM were recruited from January 1, 2014, to December 31, 2018, and participants from PURE-MIND were recruited from January 1, 2010, to December 31, 2018. Data analyses were conducted between July 16, 2024, and August 16, 2026. Exposures UPF consumption assessed using previously validated semiquantitative food frequency questionnaires and expressed as servings per 2000 kcal/d. Main Outcomes and Measures The main outcomes were body fat (BF) percentage (bioelectrical impedance), visceral adipose tissue (VAT) volume, hepatic fat fraction (HFF), VBI defined as covert brain infarcts or high white matter hyperintensities (HWMHs) (measured by MRI), and cognitive performance measured by the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MOCA) and the Digital Symbol Substitution Test (DSST). Results In this cross-sectional study of 8783 participants (mean [SD] age, 57.7 [8.7] years; 4917 females [56.6%]), those in the highest quartile of UPF intake had a BF percentage that was 1.7 (95% CI, 1.2-2.2) percentage points higher and a 5.7 (95% CI, 3.2-8.3) mL greater VAT volume compared with those in the lowest quartile, but no significant difference in HFF. Compared with the lowest quartile, the highest UPF quartile had higher odds of VBI (adjusted OR, 1.40; 95% CI, 1.10-1.77; P for trend = .009). No significant associations were observed between UPF intake and MOCA or DSST performance. Conclusions and Relevance In this cross-sectional study of middle-aged adults in Canada, higher UPF intake was associated with greater adiposity and higher odds of MRI-defined VBI but not cognitive performance. Associations with VBI were sensitive to UPF exposure definition. Longitudinal studies are needed to establish temporality.

item.title: Multi-Institutional Data for Faculty Well-Being Improvements Within and Across Medical Schools
item.dc:creator: Robert G. Badgett
Katherine Balas
Catherine F. Pipas
Jon Courand
Jennifer L. Hartwell
Valerie M. Dandar
item.description:
Authors: Robert G. Badgett, Katherine Balas, Catherine F. Pipas, Jon Courand, Jennifer L. Hartwell, Valerie M. Dandar
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2639005
Abstract: Importance Burnout, engagement, and satisfaction vary in prevalence and correlate with organizational performance in US medical colleges. Large-scale improvements have been elusive. Objective To quantify rates of well-being and its organizational correlates so to help identify opportunities for shared learning and focus well-being interventions across and within medical schools. Design, Setting, and Participants In this cross-sectional study, 28 US medical schools accredited by the Liaison Committee on Medical Education were surveyed from January 26, 2021, through June 3, 2024. Of 28 919 eligible faculty, 16 994 participated (58.8%; range, 21% to 92%). Exposure The Association of American Medical Colleges' StandPoint Faculty Engagement Survey. Main Outcomes and Measures The psychological states of burnout, satisfaction, and organizational commitment as a proxy for engagement and their antecedents. Heterogeneity beyond chance was quantified in the rates across and within schools using the I 2 statistic. Positive deviants, or bright spots, were identified as those schools and departments whose confidence intervals did not include the group mean rate. Regression analyses assessed the factors contributing to the success of the positive deviants. Results Across 15 404 respondents (9093 [53.5%] identified as men), a pooled 32% reported burnout. Across schools, there was substantial heterogeneity in rates beyond chance of burnout (13%-41%; I 2 = 75%), commitment (pooled 80% [range, 74%-95%]; I 2 = 82%), and satisfaction (pooled 77% [range, 62%-86%]; I 2 = 80%). Few departments (67 of 502 [13.3%]) had a favorable rate of both commitment and burnout. For rates of burnout at the department level, 32% of the variance was explained by the rates of burnout of their school and discipline; the rates of autonomy, purpose, and belonging; and gender and age. The burnout of individuals was explained by the mean burnout score of one’s department ( R 2 = 4%), with no contribution by the school or discipline. When combined with the factors contributing to departmental variation, 24% of the variance in burnout across individuals was explained. Conclusions and Relevance In this cross-sectional study, the substantial heterogeneity beyond chance and identification of positive deviants (bright spots) support the opportunity for learning health systems and learning communities across and within schools and professional societies to identify positive deviant departments or schools and share details of implementing existing successful practices for promoting well-being. Both burnout and engagement should be monitored within and across medical schools, as these measures may not converge.

item.title: Direct Certification With Medicaid and School Lunch Participation Among Maryland Public Schools
item.dc:creator: C. Ross Hatton
Nan Dou
Julia Gross
Raquel Arbaiza
Erin R. Hager
Susan M. Gross
item.description:
Authors: C. Ross Hatton, Nan Dou, Julia Gross, Raquel Arbaiza, Erin R. Hager, Susan M. Gross
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2638878
Abstract: Importance States may join the US Department of Agriculture Direct Certification with Medicaid (DCM) program, allowing schools to use Medicaid participation to automatically qualify students for free and reduced-price school meals (F/RP). DCM also informs the Identified Student Percentage (ISP), which determines eligibility for the Community Eligibility Provision (CEP). Pre–COVID-19 evaluations found mixed associations between DCM and school meal participation. Pandemic-era policies included free meals for all students, which has ended in most states. Therefore, a postpandemic evaluation of DCM is warranted. Objective To examine the association of Maryland’s DCM implementation in the 2022-2023 school year (SY22-23) with ISP, CEP eligibility and enrollment, and school lunch participation. Design, Setting, and Participants In this cohort study, publicly available school-level data were used to examine annual ISP, CEP participation, and school lunch participation among public schools in Maryland. A school-level fixed effects model evaluated changes in school lunch participation before (SY18-19 and SY19-20) and after (SY22-23 and SY23-24) DCM implementation among non-CEP schools. A 2-way fixed effects model tested the association between CEP enrollment and school lunch participation among schools newly eligible for CEP due to DCM. Data analyses were conducted from July to December 2025. Exposure DCM implementation. Main Outcomes and Measures ISP, CEP eligibility and enrollment, and school lunch participation. Results Among 1252 schools, 856 (68.4%) were elementary, 221 (17.7%) were middle, and 175 (14.0%) were high schools; 734 (58.6%) were suburban, 258 (20.6%) were located in rural or small towns, and 260 (20.8%) were urban. Mean (SD) ISP increased from 25.9% (17.5%) in SY21-22 to 37.3% (19.6%) in SY22-23 after DCM implementation. In SY23-24, CEP eligibility and enrollment increased by 26.7 and 22.2 percentage points, respectively. School lunch participation increased by 1.9 (95% CI, 1.1-2.8) percentage points ( P &amp;lt; .001) among non-CEP schools post-DCM (SY22-23 and SY23-24). Among schools newly participating in CEP, school lunch participation increased by 6.5 (95% CI, 4.6-8.3) percentage points ( P &amp;lt; .001). Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of Maryland public schools, DCM implementation was associated with increases in direct certification for F/RP meals, CEP participation, and lunch participation. DCM implementation may support school meal participation in the post–COVID-19 pandemic context. Programs such as CEP and Medicaid may warrant policy attention to support school meal access and its benefits for student health and academic outcomes.

item.title: Cultural Engagement and Hospital-Treated Mental Disorders in Older Adults
item.dc:creator: Pei Qin
Andrew Steptoe
Daisy Fancourt
item.description:
Authors: Pei Qin, Andrew Steptoe, Daisy Fancourt
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2639041
Abstract: Importance Cultural engagement is associated longitudinally with better mental health and reduced depression incidence, but evidence has largely relied on self-reported symptoms and diagnoses, leaving uncertainty about clinically recorded disorders, and residual confounding remains a concern. Objective To examine whether cultural engagement is associated with incident hospital-treated mental disorders. Design, Setting, and Participants This prospective cohort study included adults aged 50 years and older from the English Longitudinal Study of Aging (wave 4, May 2008 to July 2009), with follow-up through March 2024. Data were analyzed from November 2025 to March 2026. Exposures Frequency of engagement with any of the receptive arts activities (ie, watching or consuming performances or exhibitions) was categorized as never, infrequent (less than once a year up to once or twice a year), or frequent (every few months up to monthly or more). Main Outcomes and Measures Participant records were linked to diagnostic codes in Hospital Episode Statistics and mortality records with follow-up of up to 20 years. The primary outcomes were mental disorders overall and 4 main mental disorders (dementia, substance misuse, mood disorders, and neurotic disorders). Cox proportional hazard regression models were used to estimate the hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% CIs, with a false discovery rate (FDR) approach for significance. To further probe causality, eye disease, ear disease, and traumatic brain injury—which share similar sociodemographic profiles to mental disorders—were prespecified as negative control outcomes. Results This study included 8274 adults (mean [SD] age, 65.4 [9.6] years; 4672 female [55.2%]). After fully adjusting for sociodemographic, lifestyle, and social factors and multiple testing, frequent cultural engagement was associated with lower risk of any mental disorders (HR, 0.71; 95% CI, 0.62-0.82; P FDR &amp;lt; .001), dementia (HR, 0.71; 95% CI, 0.56-0.89; FDR-adjusted P = .01), substance misuse (HR, 0.75; 95% CI, 0.59-0.95; FDR-adjusted P = .04), and mood disorders (HR, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.56-0.95; FDR-adjusted P = .04), but not neurotic disorders. Associations persisted after excluding early incident cases and adjusting for baseline depressive symptoms and cognition and showed robustness to unmeasured confounders. Cultural engagement was not associated with any negative control outcomes. Conclusions and Relevance In this nationally representative cohort of older adults, cultural engagement was associated with a lower hazard of subsequent hospital-treated mental disorders, with particularly consistent associations for dementia, substance misuse, and mood disorders. These findings provide triangulated statistical data to suggest that cultural engagement is associated with reduced risk of several clinically recorded mental disorders and support further testing of cultural engagement as a population mental health strategy.

item.dc:creator: Dhruv Khurana
Maryah Garner
Sonam Khurana
Bijan Sasaninia
Anthony Firek
item.description:
Authors: Dhruv Khurana, Maryah Garner, Sonam Khurana, Bijan Sasaninia, Anthony Firek
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2638995
Abstract: Importance US federal reporting changes in 2025 removed sexual orientation and gender identity (SOGI) measures from health-center reporting, raising concerns about equity surveillance. Objective To quantify how incomplete or absent SOGI data are associated with detection of disparities in documented HIV preexposure prophylaxis (PrEP) orders. Design, Setting, and Participants This cross-sectional study used electronic health record data from a large safety-net health system in Southern California. Data were from patients 18 years or older registered as of October 28, 2025, with documented PrEP orders from January 2, 2019, through October 27, 2025. Registration dates were unavailable, precluding common follow-up. Three surveillance scenarios were assessed: complete SOGI, sex assigned at birth (SAAB) only, and joint SOGI missingness from 0% to 90%. Adults with classifiable SAAB, sexual orientation, and gender identity were included. Exposures Complete, unavailable, or partially missing SOGI data. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was any documented PrEP order. Logistic regression models adjusted for age and race and ethnicity, with interactions of sexual orientation or gender identity with SAAB. Marginally standardized probabilities and adjusted percentage-point differences were estimated within SAAB strata. Each nonzero missing level included 250 simulations to assess the magnitude, precision, and statistical detectability of each difference. Results This study included 165 198 adults (mean [SD] age, 45.0 [16.4] years). Most patients (97 621 [59.1%]) were female SAAB; 5790 (3.5%) were lesbian, gay, bisexual, or another sexual minority (LGB+) and 303 (0.2%) were transgender or gender diverse (TGD). A total of 1406 patients (0.9%) had a documented PrEP order. Under the complete SOGI analytic scenario, the adjusted probability of a documented PrEP order among cisgender patients assigned male at birth was 26.7 percentage points (pp) (95% CI, 24.9-28.5 pp; P &amp;lt; .001) higher for LGB+ patients than for heterosexual patients. Among all patients assigned male at birth, the adjusted probability was 12.3 pp (95% CI, 7.0-17.6 pp; P &amp;lt; .001) higher for TGD patients than for cisgender patients. Neither difference was significant among patients assigned female at birth. Under SAAB-only surveillance, only a difference between male and female SAAB was measurable (1.4 pp; 95% CI, 1.3-1.5 pp; P &amp;lt; .001), whereas SOGI-specific differences were not estimable. Under joint missing-completely-at-random deletion, positive-direction detectability of the male-SAAB sexual orientation difference remained at 100% through 90% missingness; detectability of the gender identity difference declined from 100% at 40% missingness to 51.6% at 80% missingness and 19.2% at 90% missingness. Selective missingness attenuated estimates. Conclusions and Relevance In this cross-sectional study, the complete SOGI analytic scenario enabled estimation of SOGI-stratified differences, whereas SAAB-only surveillance did not. Partial collection preserved estimability but reduced precision, and selective missingness attenuated estimates.

Authors: Kristine Bihrmann, Annette Kjær Ersbøll, Marie Louise Svendsen, Hanne Søndergaard, Ann-Dorthe Zwisler
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2639054
Abstract: Importance Despite clinical benefits and guideline recommendations, uptake of exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation (CR) following coronary artery disease remains suboptimal, with barriers including transportation issues, travel distance, and geographic location. To overcome these barriers, decentralization strategies that move health care to local settings have been developed across several countries. Objective To determine whether CR uptake improved following decentralization, and whether geographic and social inequalities were reduced. Design, Setting, and Participants This register-based cohort study used data from 2013 to 2022, with data analysis performed from April to August 2025. This population-based study was conducted within 21 Danish municipalities. All participants were patients aged 30 years or older discharged alive after acute myocardial infarction, percutaneous coronary intervention, or coronary artery bypass grafting. Patients were identified in the Danish National Patient Register. Patients were excluded if they had a previous diagnosis or procedure or did not reside within the study area. Exposures Travel distance from home to nearest CR facility and educational level. Main Outcomes and Measures Uptake (attending at least 1 training session within 180 days from discharge) was analyzed using modified Poisson regression to quantify differences in proportions before and after decentralization with adjustment for relevant covariates. Results A total of 19 375 patients were eligible for the study, and 295 patients with missing information on exposures or covariates were excluded. Among the included 19 080 patients, 13 355 (70.0%) were male, and 10 868 (57.0%) were aged 60 to 79 years. The median (IQR) travel distance was reduced from 15.1 (5.9-25.7) km to 7.2 (2.8-14.8) km after decentralization, and uptake increased by 16% (risk ratio [RR], 1.16; 95% CI, 1.12-1.19). Among the 20% of patients with the longest travel distance, uptake increased by 45% (RR, 1.45; 95% CI, 1.33-1.58), and geographic inequality was significantly reduced. Among patients with short education, uptake increased by 27% (RR, 1.27; 95% CI, 1.20-1.35), and social inequality was significantly reduced. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of 19 080 patients, there was increased uptake of CR after decentralization to primary care, accompanied by significant reductions in geographic and social inequalities. The findings support decentralized delivery of CR as a feasible and equitable model, but ongoing monitoring of quality and safety remains essential.

item.description:
Authors: Tait D. Shanafelt, Linda Boxer, Maryam Makowski, Mary B. Leonard, Brian T. Bateman, Euan Ashley, Hanhan Wang, Mickey Trockel
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2638946
Abstract: Importance Although US health care organizations are attempting to improve physician retention, national data indicate that physician turnover is increasing. There are minimal data on the associations between physicians’ assessment of their immediate supervisor and alignment of individual and organizational values and objective turnover. Objective To evaluate the association between individual responses from physician surveys evaluating named immediate supervisor and alignment of individual and organizational values with objective turnover during the following 2 years. Design, Setting, and Participants This cohort study included practicing physicians completing organizational surveys at a large, academic medical center between October 3, 2016, and May 1, 2024. Standardized instruments were used to assess leader behavior, alignment of individual and organizational values, burnout, and professional fulfillment at 5 survey time points. Individual survey responses were paired with human resources records on objective turnover. Exposure The 9-item Mayo Clinic Leadership Impact Index, Stanford Values Alignment Scale, Stanford Professional Fulfillment Index, and a measure of self-reported intent to leave within the next 2 years were administered. Main Outcomes and Measures Objective turnover was determined from human resource records. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to evaluate the association of leader behavior and alignment of individual and organizational values with turnover, adjusting for age, sex, survey year, and occupational well-being measures associated with turnover (ie, burnout and professional fulfillment). Results In aggregate, 7351 survey responses from 3124 unique physicians (1528 [48.9%] female) paired with 2-year objective turnover were available. The participation rate exceeded 50% in all survey years (2016: 1281 of 2392 [53.6%]; 2019: 1285 of 1924 [66.8%]; 2020: 1479 of 1909 [77.5%]; 2022: 1553 of 2251 [69.0%]; 2024: 1654 of 2498 [66.2%]) Each 1-point higher score (range, 0-10) for leader behavior (hazard ratio [HR], 0.89 [95% CI, 0.85-0.93]; P &amp;lt; .001) and values alignment (HR, 0.90 [95% CI, 0.86-0.94]; P &amp;lt; .001) was associated with decreased objective 2-year turnover. After adjusting for age, sex, survey year, values alignment, occupational burnout, and professional fulfillment, each 1-point difference in leadership behavior score (HR, 0.88 [95% CI, 0.83-0.94]; P &amp;lt; .001) remained associated with objective 2-year turnover. The association between values alignment and 2-year objective turnover was no longer present in these analyses. On paired individual-level data from physicians completing consecutive surveys and adjusting for baseline score, each 1-point increase in leader behavior (HR, 0.82 [95% CI, 0.76-0.90]; P &amp;lt; .001) and values alignment (HR, 0.86 [95% CI, 0.79-0.93]; P &amp;lt; .001) score between surveys was associated with reduced turnover following the second survey. On multivariable analysis adjusting for age, sex, and survey year, respondents indicating moderate (HR, 3.22 [95% CI, 2.41-4.31]) or likely to definite intent to leave (HR, 8.58 [95% CI, 6.43-11.44]; P &amp;lt; .001) were at higher risk of objective 2-year turnover. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study, physician evaluation of immediate supervisor behavior and alignment between individual and organizational values on organizational surveys were associated with subsequent objective turnover. These findings suggest that organizations seeking to promote physician retention should conduct leadership assessments, attend to leadership development, and foster values alignment with their physicians.

item.title: Out-of-Pocket Costs for Chronic Illness Management in High-Deductible Health Plans
item.dc:creator: Risha Gidwani
Zachary Wagner
Steven M. Asch
Veronica Yank
Lane Burgette
item.description:
Authors: Risha Gidwani, Zachary Wagner, Steven M. Asch, Veronica Yank, Lane Burgette
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2638780
Abstract: Importance High-deductible health plans (HDHPs) enroll a substantial share of privately insured Americans and are associated with reduced use of care, even care that is considered medically necessary. However, the magnitude of patient out-of-pocket (OOP) costs required to obtain evidence-based medical care when enrolled in HDHPs remains poorly understood. Objective To estimate patient OOP costs required to receive guideline-concordant care for common chronic conditions when enrolled in an HDHP vs a non-HDHP. Design, Setting, and Participants This retrospective cohort study used 2022 to 2023 national commercial insurance claims data. Participants included adults aged 18 to 64 years with employer-sponsored insurance and previously diagnosed diabetes, hypertension, or both. To enter the cohort, persons had to have received guideline-concordant care for their chronic illnesses. Data were analyzed from July 2025 to April 2026. Exposure Enrollment in an HDHP vs a non-HDHP. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was annual patient OOP costs to receive evidence-based care. Entropy balancing and generalized linear models with geographic fixed effects estimated the mean OOP costs of receiving minimum recommended medical care for diabetes, hypertension, or both in HDHPs and non-HDHPs. Estimates were weighted to ensure that observed costs were representative of the full sample of chronically ill persons. Results There were 539 590 adults receiving guideline-concordant care who entered the cohort. After entropy balancing, groups exhibited mean covariate balance, with males representing 57.9% of HDHP enrollees and 57.8% of non-HDHP enrollees, and similar age distributions across groups, with 45.4% of both HDHP and non-HDHP enrollees 55 to 64 years of age. The estimated annual OOP cost for individuals to receive guideline-concordant diabetes care was $153.91 (95% CI, $150.18-$157.64) in HDHPs vs $68.06 (95% CI, $66.34-$69.78) in non-HDHPs; $128.94 (95% CI, $127.25-$130.64) in HDHPs vs $53.89 (95% CI, $53.20-$54.58) in non-HDHPs for guideline-concordant hypertension care; and $164.18 (95% CI, $160.93-$167.44) in HDHPs vs $100.60 (95% CI, $98.80-$102.39) in non-HDHPs for guideline-concordant care for comorbid diabetes and hypertension (all P &amp;lt; .001). Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of a large, national sample of chronically ill adults with hypertension, diabetes, or both, annual patient costs were 1.6 to 2.4 times as high to receive recommended care in HDHPs vs non-HDHPs, although the magnitude of the difference in OOP costs was relatively small (range, $63.68 to $85.85). Findings provide novel evidence quantifying the magnitude of cost burden experienced by chronically ill patients under various insurance mechanisms and complement prior HDHP studies evaluating health care utilization.

item.description:
Authors: Alicia I. Rolin, Robert McCarter, Gia M. Badolato, Meleah D. Boyle, Thevaasiinen Chandereng, David Branson, Brittney Boakye, James M. Chamberlain, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2638552
Abstract: Importance Heightened immigration enforcement in the US has been associated with reduced health care utilization in immigrant communities. Pediatric emergency departments (EDs) serve as a critical safety net for children, yet the impacts of acute immigration enforcement activity in pediatric ED utilization remain incompletely characterized. Objective To evaluate whether deployment of federal law enforcement in Washington, DC, was associated with changes in pediatric ED utilization and whether these changes differed by the patients’ preferred language, race, and ethnicity. Design, Setting, and Participants This repeated cross-sectional interrupted time series analysis compared daily pediatric ED visits from June 1 to September 30, 2025, with visits in the same calendar period in 2024 at a single pediatric ED at a freestanding children’s hospital in Washington, DC. Participants included all patients younger than 26 years presenting to the pediatric ED during the study period. Exposures Deployment of federal law enforcement personnel, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement and National Guard troops, in Washington, DC, beginning August 11, 2025. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was daily pediatric ED visit counts. Interrupted time series models estimated immediate changes in ED utilization and postdeployment trends by patient-preferred language, race, and ethnicity, adjusting for age, sex, and acuity. Results A total of 21 822 pediatric ED visits were included in the analysis (median age, 6.5 [IQR, 2.0-13.1] years; 11 505 visits [52.7%] by male patients). Among these visits, 6253 patients (28.7%) identified as Hispanic, 10 649 (48.8%) as non-Hispanic Black, 2200 (10.1%) as non-Hispanic White, 558 (2.6%) as non-Hispanic multiracial, 1411 (6.5%) as non-Hispanic additional race, and 652 (3.0%), unknown. Patients who preferred to speak Spanish experienced an estimated immediate change in visits following federal deployment of −10.4 visits per day, whereas patients who preferred English experienced an estimated immediate change of 5.6 visits per day (difference, −16.0 visits per day). Hispanic patients similarly experienced an estimated immediate change of −13.3 visits per day, whereas non-Hispanic patients experienced an estimated immediate change of 6.2 visits per day (difference, −19.4 visits per day). Among Hispanic patients, those preferring Spanish had greater estimated immediate changes (−12.1 visits per day) than those preferring English (−0.8 visits per day; difference, −11.3 visits per day). No significant differences were observed across non-Hispanic racial and ethnic groups. No comparable declines were observed during the same period in 2024. Conclusion and Relevance In this repeated cross-sectional study of pediatric ED visits before and after a federal immigration enforcement deployment, heightened immigration enforcement activity was associated with an immediate reduction in pediatric ED utilization, particularly among patients who preferred to speak Spanish. These findings suggest that immigration enforcement may have unintended consequences for children’s use of emergency care.

item.title: Patient Navigation Plus mHealth Incentives for Linkage to OUD Care for Adults Who Also Use Methamphetamines
item.dc:creator: Elenore P. Bhatraju
Kaitlin A. Zinsli
Devin N. Kennedy
Alexander J. Gojic
Matthew Iles-Shih
Joseph O. Merrill

item.description:
Authors: Elenore P. Bhatraju, Kaitlin A. Zinsli, Devin N. Kennedy, Alexander J. Gojic, Matthew Iles-Shih, Joseph O. Merrill, Elizabeth C. Speaker, Jeffrey H. Samet, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2638542
Abstract: Importance Hospitalization is common among people with opioid use disorder (OUD) and is recognized as a reachable moment to start treatment. Methamphetamine use among people with OUD is associated with decreased linkage to postdischarge OUD care. Objective To determine the feasibility, acceptability, and exploratory clinical outcomes of a pilot randomized clinical trial (RCT) of an adherence-focused mobile health (mHealth) intervention aiming to increase linkage to and retention in outpatient buprenorphine services for patients hospitalized with OUD and methamphetamine use. Design, Setting, and Participants This single-site, 2-arm pilot RCT was conducted from January 3, 2024, to April 14, 2025, at a single-site, large urban safety net hospital in Seattle, Washington. Patients 18 years or older were eligible if they had initiated buprenorphine for OUD while in the hospital and had used methamphetamine within the past 30 days. Participants were randomized to the mHealth Incentivized Adherence Plus Patient Navigation (MIAPP) intervention or to treatment as usual (TAU). Intervention The MIAPP intervention combined financial incentives via mHealth-based adherence monitoring with a patient navigator (PN) during the first 30 days after discharge. Main Outcomes and Measures Feasibility was assessed by meeting the target enrollment of 40 participants and intervention delivery. Acceptability was measured by patient satisfaction ratings on a scale from 0 to 10, with 0 indicating not at all satisfied and 10 indicating extremely satisfied. The main pilot clinical outcome was linkage to outpatient OUD care within 30 days of hospital discharge, defined as medications for OUD being prescribed or dispensed. Other outcomes included retention in buprenorphine treatment and hospital readmissions at 90 days; past 30-day methamphetamine use was measured at the 30-day follow-up visit. Results The target enrollment of 40 participants (mean [SD] age, 43.4 [12.6] years) was met. Most participants (33 [82.5%]) were male. The intervention was allocated to 20 participants and delivered to 19 (95.0%); 20 participants received TAU. Participants reported being highly satisfied with the PN, with a mean (SD) patient satisfaction rating of 9.9 (0.3). Linkage to OUD care at 30 days occurred in 11 participants (55.0%) in the intervention arm compared with 10 (50.0%) in the TAU arm (risk ratio, 1.10; 95% CI, 0.61-1.99). Conclusions and Relevance In this pilot RCT of the MIAPP intervention, study procedures were feasible and acceptable. While no difference in linkage rates was noted in this pilot study, larger studies are needed to determine intervention effectiveness. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06027814

item.dc:creator: Natasha Steele

Vishnu Nair

item.description:
Authors: Natasha Steele, Amrapali Maitra, Zhiyong Dong, Deborah Wachenheim, Vishnu Nair, Alfredo Reyes-Guzman, Aditya Narayan, Erika Schillinger, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2638695
Abstract: Importance The 21st Century Cures Act made clinical notes broadly accessible to patients. However, the frequency and patient-perceived consequences of disrespectful or judgmental language (DJL) in medical records among the general US population remain unknown. Objectives To (1) quantify the frequency of participant-reported DJL in medical records; (2) characterize patient-anticipated consequences; and (3) examine factors associated with DJL and documentation trust in clinicians. Design, Setting, and Participants Cross-sectional, nationally weighted survey of 500 US adults conducted from November 21 to December 4, 2025, using YouGov’s nonprobability-based online panel. Main Outcomes and Measures Descriptive statistics characterized experience of DJL in medical records (patient portal users) or health care (nonportal users) and patient-anticipated consequences. Adjusted odds ratios (aORs) and 95% CIs were estimated using multivariable logistic regression including sociodemographics and clinical factors for 2 outcomes: DJL and documentation trust. Results Among 500 respondents (mean [SE] age, 48.0 [0.9] years; 253 [51.0%] women, 53 [11.0%] Black, 80 [18.0%] Hispanic [any race], and 315 [60.0%] White, 358 portal users [71.2%]), a total of 83 participants reported DJL: 58 of 358 (17.1%) portal users in their own medical records and/or that of a loved one, and 25 of 142 nonportal users (15.6%) in health care encounters. Patient-reported consequences included 377 of 500 respondents (74.7%) who anticipated DJL would influence subsequent care from a new clinician, and 373 (73.3%) who anticipated worse health outcomes, such as wrong medication prescribing or diagnostic errors. Furthermore, 435 of 500 respondents (85.5%) anticipated they would be less likely to return to the clinician. In adjusted analyses, patients who reported low income (compared with high income: aOR, 2.64; 95% CI, 1.18-5.91; P = .03) had a greater likelihood of reporting DJL, as did those with a diagnosis of chronic pain (compared with no diagnosis of chronic pain: aOR, 3.25; 95% CI, 1.46-7.26; P = .004). The experience of DJL was associated with diminished documentation trust in clinicians (aOR, 5.76; 95% CI, 2.90-11.46; P &amp;lt; .001). Conclusions and Relevance In this survey study, 1 in 6 US adults reported DJL in medical records (or in health care experiences for nonportal users), disproportionately affecting those with low income or chronic pain, and DJL was associated with diminished clinician documentation trust. Patient-anticipated consequences such as diminished intent to return to clinician suggest important quality of care and system-level implications. Realizing the promise of health information transparency will require concurrent reform in respectful language in clinical documentation and health care encounters.

item.title: Trends in Violence Against Children in Australia
item.dc:creator: Lucinda Grummitt
Siobhan O’Dean
Tim Slade
item.description:
Authors: Lucinda Grummitt, Siobhan O’Dean, Tim Slade
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2638285
Abstract: Importance Administrative data are commonly used to monitor multiple forms of violence against children, within and external to the family, yet different systems capture distinct thresholds of harm. Reliance on single data sources may obscure population-level trends. Objective To examine trends in multiple indicators of children’s exposure to violence in Australia from 2014 to 2024 and to assess whether trends differ across police, health, and child protection data sources. Design, Setting, and Participants This cohort study used a time-trend analysis of Australian national administrative data spanning from 2014 to 2024. Data sources included national police-recorded assaults, hospitalizations, and child protection data from 3 Australian national agency databases. Participants were children aged 0 to 17 years, disaggregated by sex and age group. Analyses were conducted from January to April 2026. Exposures Year, modeled continuously. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcomes were annual rates per 100 000 population on police-recorded sexual assault, family and domestic violence (FDV)–related assault, hospitalizations for assault, and child maltreatment substantiations. Temporal trends were modeled using quasi-Poisson regression with population offsets, and average annual percentage changes were estimated. Turning points were assessed using Davies test and segmented regression. Results Annual population denominators ranged from 2.6 to 2.8 million girls and 2.7 to 3.0 million boys aged 0 to 17 years. Police-recorded sexual assault rates increased steadily among girls aged 0 to 9 years (2.8% per year; 95% CI, 2.0% to 3.6% per year) and those aged 10 to 17 years (4.2% per year; 95% CI, 3.4% to 5.0% per year). Among boys aged 10 to 17 years, rates accelerated sharply after 2021 (15.7% per year; 95% CI, 5.5% to 26.9% per year). FDV-related assault showed a similar trend, with stable to modest increases before 2021 followed by steep increases thereafter. Assault-related hospitalizations were generally stable, except for declines among boys aged 10 to 17 years (−1.4% per year; 95% CI, −2.7% to −0.1% per year). Overall child maltreatment substantiation remained stable, but declines were found for physical (−3.2% per year; 95% CI, −5.2% to −1.2% year) and sexual (−3.6% per year; 95% CI, −5.2% to −2.0% per year) abuse, alongside an increase in emotional abuse substantiations to 2020 (7.6% per year; 95% CI, 5.2% to 10.0% per year), followed by a decline (−7.0% per year; 95% CI, −11.8% to −1.9% per year). Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study using Australian national administrative data, trends in violence against children differed substantially across systems. Although police data indicated increased violence exposure, particularly in recent years, child-protection substantiations and hospitalizations remained stable or declined. Strengthened national surveillance is critical.
